statement: The book develops a unified foundation for distributed problem solving, game-theoretic interaction, learning, communication, mechanisms, coalitions, and epistemic logic.
limits: A synthesis, not one empirical MARL study

statement: Theorem 3.3.22 states that every game with finitely many players and finitely many actions has at least one mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium.
limits: Existence does not provide an efficient learning or computation method

statement: Theorem 4.2.1 states that finding a sample Nash equilibrium of a finite general-sum game with two or more players is PPAD-complete.
limits: PPAD-completeness is not NP-completeness and does not prove every instance hard

statement: Theorems 6.4.5 and 6.4.6 establish that finite exact potential games have pure-strategy Nash equilibria and that congestion games are potential games.
conditions: Finite exact potential game for the existence result
Congestion-game construction for the representation result
limits: Does not imply arbitrary Markov games are potential games

statement: Theorem 7.4.2 presents Q-learning convergence under the stated infinite visitation and learning-rate conditions for a finite unknown MDP.
conditions: Every state-action pair visited infinitely often
Learning rates satisfy the stated stochastic-approximation conditions
limits: Single-agent MDP result; later multi-agent variants require extra structure

statement: The communication chapter distinguishes cheap talk, signaling through action, and speech-act accounts, while the logic chapters formalize knowledge, common knowledge, belief, and group intention.
limits: No bandwidth-constrained neural communication experiment

statement: The book's n-player formulations and separately analyzed games do not demonstrate held-out-N generalization by one frozen learned policy, and the text does not define an adaptive HMASD skill period k.
limits: Do not relabel player-count parameters or repeated-game horizons as HMASD axes

statement: Potential functions, stochastic-game state models, communication semantics, and common-knowledge distinctions are prospective ingredients for specifying an HMASD coordination mechanism and its information assumptions.
conditions: A target HMASD model must justify each imported assumption
limits: No project result is evidence for the textbook and vice versa

statement: Definition 2 presents a Dec-POMDP as a cooperative multiagent stochastic control model with shared reward, joint actions, stochastic transitions and observations, and locally conditioned policies.
limits: The later Definition 10 makes communication/agent-model components more explicit

statement: Theorem 1 states that finding an optimal finite-horizon Dec-POMDP solution for n at least 2 is NEXP-complete, and the surrounding text reports the same worst-case class for epsilon-approximation.
limits: Worst-case complexity does not characterize every structured instance

statement: Theorem 2 states that the finite-horizon plan-time optimal value function is piecewise-linear and convex in the plan-time sufficient statistic.
limits: Representation size can still be prohibitive

statement: Infinite-horizon solutions are represented with finite-state controllers and optimized using policy iteration, bounded policy iteration, nonlinear programming, expectation maximization, or NOMDP reductions.
conditions: Finite controller approximations for practical methods
limits: Not a single universally optimal algorithm

statement: Section 8.2 treats macro-actions as temporally extended lower-level policies selected by a higher-level policy to make long-horizon planning more tractable.
limits: Does not make duration adaptive by itself

statement: Section 8.3 distinguishes implicit and explicit communication and covers instantaneous, one-step delayed, k-step delayed, costly, and local communication.
conditions: Communication model and semantics must be stated
limits: The k-step delay is a fixed information delay

statement: Fixed k-step communication delay is not evidence for an adaptive skill period k, and solving separate Dec-POMDPs with different agent counts is not one-policy variable-N generalization.
conditions: Bounded to terminology in this book
limits: Do not map delay or instance size directly to HMASD claims

statement: Local-history policies, plan-time sufficient statistics, factored coordination graphs, macro-actions, and communication costs are prospective components for an information-explicit UAV Dec-POMDP benchmark.
conditions: The target benchmark must define observations, communication, action timing, and comparator
limits: No direct empirical UAV result in this book

statement: The authors argue that several distinct multi-agent-learning agendas are often implicit and conflated, which makes results difficult to evaluate and compare.
conditions: Based on the authors' reading of the literature
limits: A position claim, not an empirical frequency estimate

statement: The paper groups common result types into equilibrium convergence in self-play, successful opponent-model learning, and achieving a payoff threshold.
conditions: Selective sample of prior MAL work
limits: Not an exhaustive classification

statement: The five proposed agendas are computational, descriptive, normative, prescriptive cooperative, and prescriptive non-cooperative.
conditions: Each agenda has a different motivation and success criterion
limits: Authors allow that additional agendas may exist

statement: For prescriptive cooperative learning, the authors propose evaluating joint-policy value together with computation, communication, or learning time rather than equilibrium deviation incentives.
limits: Does not specify a particular benchmark or estimator

statement: Convergence to an equilibrium or no-regret behavior is not automatically evidence of task performance; the question and yardstick must be fixed before comparing algorithms.
limits: Does not reject equilibrium or regret when they match the intended question

statement: For HMASD, state whether a variable-N or variable-k study is computational, descriptive, normative, cooperative-control, or adversarial-agent design, then choose matched robustness/performance metrics.
conditions: Connection is a design use of the taxonomy
limits: No HMASD experiment appears in the source

statement: Definition 2 defines a Markov potential game by equality between every unilateral policy-change difference in an agent value and the corresponding state-dependent potential difference.
conditions: Equality holds for every agent, state, and compared policy
limits: MPG structure must be proved or modeled; it is not generic

statement: Lemma 2.1 and Remark 2 express independent NPG as an advantage-logit update and, in policy coordinates, as multiplicative weights.
limits: Does not address sampling error or function approximation

statement: Theorem 3.1 states last-iterate convergence to equilibrium policies when every agent runs INPG with step size below the stated (1-gamma)^3/(27 n^2 A_max^2 M) threshold.
conditions: Interior initialization; isolated fixed points invoked in Lemma 3.6
limits: Asymptotic result; no finite-time rate
Oracle advantages
MPG only

statement: The proof route identifies INPG with natural ascent on the potential, proves monotonic potential improvement, and then relates fixed points to equilibrium policies.
limits: Lemma 3.6's isolated-fixed-point condition is material

statement: In the four-agent stochastic congestion experiment, the authors report about 2,000 iterations for IPG versus about 50 for INPG under the selected tabular setup and learning rate 0.0001.
conditions: L1 distance to each run's final policy
limits: No train/test split
Oracle/tabular updates
Iteration counts are environment-specific
One policy does not cross N

statement: The experiments separately instantiate 4-agent and 8-agent systems; they do not test a frozen policy across roster sizes or an in-episode membership change.
limits: No held-out-N generalization claim

statement: The MPG potential can serve prospectively as an HMASD learning-dynamics observable when a UAV coordination model has verified unilateral-difference alignment.
conditions: Need an explicit proof or diagnostic for approximate potential structure
limits: The source does not validate UAV transfer

statement: The paper defines hidden bilinear games whose parameter vectors are separately mapped through smooth functions before entering a bilinear zero-sum payoff.
conditions: Separate smooth maps F and G
limits: Does not capture all GAN or MARL interactions

statement: Theorem 3 states that, for safe initial conditions in the two-strategy hidden bilinear system, the continuous-time GDA orbit is periodic.
limits: Not a statement about arbitrary nonconvex games or unsafe initializations

statement: Theorem 4 states that time averages of the mapped strategies and expected utility converge to their Nash-equilibrium values in the two-strategy safe-initialization setting.
conditions: Conditions of the two-strategy system and safe initialization
limits: Last iterates remain periodic; averaging is essential

statement: Theorems 6-7 connect higher-dimensional trajectories to Poincare recurrence, with Theorem 7 requiring sigmoid maps or the stated one-to-one safe-map condition.
conditions: Additional map conditions for full-flow recurrence
limits: Recurrence does not imply convergence

statement: Theorems 8 and 10 construct continuous- and discrete-time systems where a positive-measure set of initial conditions converges to fixed points that are not equilibria of the hidden game.
conditions: Selected learning rate for the discrete theorem
limits: Existence counterexample, not prevalence across all games

statement: The negative results are bounded to hidden bilinear zero-sum structure and cannot be cited as proof that every general-sum MARL optimizer cycles or converges spuriously.
limits: No generic MARL impossibility theorem

statement: Cycling, energy drift, and initialization-dependent fixed points are prospective diagnostics for HMASD optimizers with rotational components; candidate repairs require separate evidence.
conditions: Mechanism must exhibit a comparable vector field
limits: No repair is tested here

statement: The paper formulates a monotone variational inequality and an equivalent strong form for continuous monotone operators on a closed convex set.
limits: Equivalence need not hold outside the stated regularity

statement: The dual extrapolation step uses a strongly convex prox geometry, two prox evaluations, and an accumulated dual linear model; Theorem 1 supplies the one-step descent inequalities for Lipschitz or bounded-variation operators.
conditions: Differentiable strongly convex prox on the relevant image
Step-size condition for the Lipschitz case
limits: Displayed equations should be checked on the source pages

statement: Theorem 2 bounds the restricted merit of the averaged iterate by LD/[sigma(k+1)] and gives at most order LD/(sigma epsilon) iterations for the Lipschitz-monotone regime.
limits: Merit is restricted by D; constants depend on geometry

statement: Theorem 3 gives an O(1/sqrt(k+1)) merit bound and O(1/epsilon^2) iteration count for monotone operators with bounded variation.
limits: Slower than the Lipschitz regime

statement: Theorem 6 specializes dual extrapolation to bilinear matrix games and bounds the restricted primal-dual gap by 4L sqrt(D1 D2/(sigma1 sigma2))/(k+1).
limits: Needs two matrix-vector products per iteration as discussed by the author

statement: The O(1/epsilon) guarantee is not a generic promise for nonmonotone, nonconvex-nonconcave, or sampled MARL learning dynamics.
conditions: Monotonicity and oracle model are essential
limits: No stochastic MARL experiment

statement: Dual extrapolation is a prospective HMASD optimizer component if a direction-specific game operator is shown to be monotone or approximately monotone under the chosen metric and constraints.
conditions: Requires a matched VI operator and oracle
limits: The paper does not supply a UAV or MARL host

statement: The analysis is for finite static exact-potential games, described by the authors as a stepping stone toward the Markov setting.
limits: Not a Markov potential-game theorem

statement: Algorithm 1 performs symmetric parallel independent NPG updates using each agent's marginalized utility and entropy-regularized multiplicative policy update.
conditions: Uniform initialization in the stated procedure
limits: Exact utility feedback rather than sampled MARL trajectories

statement: Theorem 3.1 bounds the time-average QRE gap under the stated step-size condition, yielding sublinear convergence of average iterates.
conditions: Step size at most the stated bound
limits: Average-gap result; not last-iterate linear convergence

statement: Corollary 3.2 gives O(min{sqrt(N),Phi_max} Phi_max/(tau^2 epsilon^2)) iterations for average epsilon-QRE gap from uniform initialization.
limits: Constants/log factors and average gap matter

statement: Choosing tau proportional to epsilon/log|A| yields a tilde-O(min{sqrt(N),Phi_max} Phi_max/epsilon^4) average approximate-NE guarantee; for bounded identical-interest games Phi_max=1 makes the rate dimension-free up to logarithms.
conditions: Bounded identical-interest special case for dimension-free statement
limits: Does not give a generic linear rate
Static game only

statement: The numerical study uses N=4, 20 actions, Beta(1/2,1/2) potential entries, 10 runs, and compares direct PG with NPG at several entropy values over 30,000 iterations.
limits: No train/test split
One fixed roster
No policy crosses N
Preprint experiment

statement: A rate whose expression depends favorably on N is not empirical or formal evidence that one learned policy transfers to unseen agent counts; the paper fixes one static game dimension per run.
conditions: Separate complexity scaling from cross-N generalization
limits: No held-out-N or membership-change protocol

statement: Definition 1 characterizes nonmonotonic joint Q-functions through action orderings that change with other agents' actions, exposing a class QMIX's monotonic factorization cannot represent exactly.
limits: Representational impossibility alone does not force every learned policy to be suboptimal

statement: Theorems 1-2 construct n-player k-action matrix games where QMIX learns a suboptimal policy under uniform or epsilon-greedy visitation, with the latter giving a finite-time probability bound.
limits: Counterexample family, not all cooperative tasks
The k symbol is action count

statement: MAVEN samples a shared latent z from a hierarchical policy at the start of an episode and conditions agent utilities and the mixing network on z to create episode-persistent joint exploration modes.
conditions: Shared latent available for conditioned decentralized action selection
limits: Duration is fixed to the episode

statement: The variational mutual-information objective lower-bounds I(trajectory;z) using a learned posterior q(z|trajectory) and encourages z-distinguishable trajectories.
limits: A poor posterior creates a gap; diversity/optimality is not guaranteed

statement: In the 10-step matrix game, MAVEN reaches the optimal return 13 while QMIX remains at return 10 over 100,000 training steps, summarized across 20 random initializations.
limits: Designed toy task
No held-out N or k
No separate test distribution

statement: SMAC training is paused every 100,000 steps for 32 decentralized greedy evaluation episodes, with median win rate and interquartile shading; MAVEN is compared to QMIX, QTRAN, COMA, and IQL on named maps.
limits: Map-specific training
No frozen-policy cross-roster evaluation

statement: The shared latent lasts a fixed episode and is not an adaptive skill period; the k in Theorems 1-2 denotes action count, not temporal duration.
conditions: Respect source notation and rollout protocol
limits: No externally varied or learned skill duration

statement: MAVEN's persistent latent modes and MI diversity are prospective ingredients for a variable-duration HMASD skill mechanism only after adding termination/duration control and testing changed k with one policy.
conditions: Must define duration intervention and matched comparator
limits: Current evidence covers fixed episodes

statement: Equation (1) presents the p-Wasserstein distance as an infimum over couplings between two probability distributions under a ground cost.
limits: A metric definition alone is not a MARL algorithm

statement: The paper proposes five OT-MARL application areas: policy alignment, resource management, non-stationarity, scalable learning, and energy efficiency.
limits: No implementation or empirical validation

statement: Equations (2)-(3) propose minimizing pairwise Wasserstein distances between policy-induced distributions as a policy-alignment objective.
limits: No convergence or task-performance guarantee
Objective may collapse useful specialization if used naively

statement: Equations (6)-(8) propose measuring consecutive state-distribution shift with Wasserstein distance and mapping it to an adaptive policy learning rate.
conditions: Chosen mapping f from distance to learning rate
limits: No specified estimator, stability analysis, or experiment

statement: The challenges section identifies high-dimensional computational cost and repeated recalibration as obstacles, and suggests entropic approximation plus decentralized or hierarchical decomposition.
limits: Suggested remedies are not evaluated

statement: The paper contains no theorem, benchmark, sample size, or result showing that OT improves MARL performance, robustness, scalability, or held-out-N generalization.
limits: Treat benefits as hypotheses

statement: A high-information HMASD test could compare a specified Wasserstein change observable or OT task allocator against a matched non-OT baseline under roster/distribution shifts, with compute cost included.
conditions: Fix ground cost, estimator, intervention, comparator, and resource budget
limits: Prospective design only

statement: The paper contrasts polynomial learning rates alpha_t=1/t^omega for omega in (1/2,1) with the linear rate 1/t in finite discounted tabular Q-learning.
limits: Terminology 'linear' refers to 1/t, not function approximation

statement: Theorem 2 gives a high-probability synchronous-Q-learning upper bound for polynomial learning rates with polynomial dependence on 1/(1-gamma).
limits: Bound is tabular and synchronous

statement: Theorems 4-5 extend the comparison to asynchronous Q-learning and introduce explicit dependence on exploration covering time L.
limits: Covering-time assumption can be strong and environment/policy dependent

statement: Theorem 6 and Lemma 39 construct a deterministic one-state zero-reward MDP where Q-learning with alpha_t=1/t needs order (1/epsilon)^(1/(1-gamma)) steps before sup-norm error falls below epsilon.
limits: Constructed worst case; not a universal empirical runtime

statement: Experiments use random and line MDPs with two actions per state, including 100-state 10^8-step and 10-state 10^7-step runs, and show degradation of the 1/t schedule as gamma approaches one.
limits: No uncertainty intervals or seed counts stated
Single-agent tabular setting

statement: These bounds do not transfer directly to independent MARL because other agents make the effective environment nonstationary and break the fixed Bellman contraction/sampling model.
limits: No MARL theorem in the source

statement: The gamma-by-schedule interaction is a prospective HMASD control variable: matched optimizer comparisons should hold discount, visitation, and update-count conventions fixed before attributing learning-dynamics effects.
limits: Does not identify a multi-agent repair

statement: The finite-n model consists of multi-class controlled diffusions weakly coupled through 1/n empirical averages in dynamics and individual costs.
limits: Not a discrete-time learned MARL policy model

statement: The NCE methodology solves an HJB best-response problem under a candidate measure flow and a closed-loop McKean-Vlasov system, requiring the induced measure flow to equal the candidate.
limits: A fixed point must exist and satisfy regularity conditions

statement: Theorem 5 gives a unique bounded classical HJB solution when H1-H4 hold and the measure flow belongs to the stated regularity class.
limits: Does not by itself establish NCE consistency

statement: Theorem 10 gives existence and uniqueness of the NCE equation system under H1-H6 and the composite-gain condition c1 c2 < 1.
limits: Strong regularity/gain assumptions are essential

statement: Theorem 12 bounds the difference between each coupled finite-n state process and its independent McKean-Vlasov counterpart by O(n^-1/2+epsilon_n), for first and second moments over the finite horizon.
limits: Constant may depend on horizon
State-process approximation, not learned-policy generalization

statement: Theorem 13 bounds unilateral improvement by O(n^-1/2+epsilon_n) for decentralized Lipschitz deviations when H0-H6 and an NCE feedback family hold; Corollary 14 extends epsilon-Nash to the wider strategy space for additional decomposable dynamics and costs.
limits: Asymptotic epsilon-Nash, not exact finite-n Nash
Model-based feedback rather than trained neural policy

statement: Population-limit and epsilon-Nash statements do not demonstrate that one frozen learned MARL policy executes across held-out N; they support a model-based asymptotic interface under weak-coupling assumptions.
conditions: Distinguish approximation theory from policy generalization
limits: No held-out roster experiment or in-episode churn

statement: Empirical population measures and class-conditioned feedback are prospective HMASD variable-N primitives for UAV swarms when exchangeability/weak coupling are defensible and finite-n errors are measured against a matched baseline.
conditions: Need one parameterization across N plus held-out size
limits: Prospective transfer; no UAV validation in source
